entities.summary:
Peter Krešimir IV, King of Croatia and Dalmatia from 1059 until his death in 1074, presided over the zenith of the medieval Croatian kingdom, earning the epithet 'the Great'. As the last ruler of the Krešimirović branch of the Trpimirović dynasty, his reign marked a period of significant territorial expansion, consolidation of royal authority, and enhanced international standing, particularly through adept diplomacy with the powerful Papacy under Gregory VII. He effectively united the Croatian heartland with the strategically vital Dalmatian coastal cities, previously under Byzantine nominal suzerainty, establishing a unified realm that stretched from the Drava River to the Adriatic Sea.

During his fifteen-year reign, Peter Krešimir IV strategically leveraged the ongoing Investiture Controversy to strengthen his position against both Byzantine and Venetian influence. He skillfully negotiated with Pope Alexander II and later Gregory VII, securing papal recognition for his sovereignty over Dalmatia and the right to appoint bishops, thereby asserting independence from the Patriarchate of Constantinople. The Synod of Split in 1060, though initially met with resistance, initiated Latinization reforms within the Croatian church, bringing it closer to Rome. His naval power also grew, allowing him to project influence across the Adriatic and maintain control over key maritime routes.
